newsitem.title: USA: Simpson jury decides on punitive damages.
newsitem.headline: Simpson jury decides on punitive damages.

text.p: Jurors in O.J. Simpson's civil trial reached a decision on Monday about whether to force him to pay punitive damages for the deaths of his ex-wife and her friend.

Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki summoned participants in the case to the courtoom for the final, decisive phase of the four-month trial. A court spokeswoman said the jury's decision would be read in open court at about 4:30 p.m. EST (2130 GMT).

It took jurors about five hours over two days to reach their finding, six days after they blamed Simpson for the June 1994 murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman and ordered him to pay $8.5 million in compensatory damages.

In an impassioned closing argument on Friday, Daniel Petrocelli, the plaintiffs' lead attorney, urged jurors to impose stiff punitive damages and declare to the world that "You cannot kill two people and get away with it."
But defence attorney Robert Baker contended Simpson had already been punished enough and said anything more would effectively "destroy" his client.

Simpson was cleared of murder charges in October 1995 but the victims' families pressed ahead with a wrongful-death lawsuit in civil court. The $8.5 million in compensatory damages was awarded to Goldman's divorced parents. The lawsuit filed by Nicole Brown Simpson's estate did not seek such damages but her heirs would share in any punitive damages.

As the jurors deliberated in a cramped, windowless room in the Santa Monica courthouse, police went on alert in case trouble breaks out when the decision is announced. Mounted Santa Monica police officers took up positions outside the Doubletree Guest Suites a block from the courthouse where the plaintiffs and their lawyers were to hold a news conference.
Officers were also preparing to set up barricades and seal off streets in the area.

The jury last week heard widely conflicting accounts of Simpson's financial status. His defence lawyers claimed he was more than $9 million in debt, including the $8.5 million in compensatory damages, while lawyers for the plaintiffs sought to show that Simpson had a net worth of more than $15 million and could earn $2 million to $3 million a year with product endorsements and autograph signings.

Meanwhile, Los Angeles police said the county Department of Children received an anonymous call shortly after last Tuesday's verdicts were announced that Simpson's two children by his ex-wife, Sydney and Justin, "might be in danger."
A police spokesman said social workers went to Simpson's mansion, found the children safe and determined the call was a hoax.
